frames.narration: The app asks for people user 5 may know: friends of friends, ranked by the number of friends in common, top 20. The query API sets limits of 2 hops and 50,000 edges, and hands it to a traversal engine.
User 5 is on shard 2 of 4. The engine reads the node's adjacency list: a direct read of 180 neighbour ids with no index lookup and no join.

The guard looks at the stored degree of each friend. One of them is a celebrity with 2,000,000 followers. The engine will keep that friend in the result but will not open the list, so 179 friends are expanded.

The friends are spread by hash over four shards, so about three quarters, roughly 134 of the 179, live elsewhere. The engine sends one batched request per shard, three requests in parallel, rather than 134 separate calls.

Each shard returns its adjacency lists. At about 190 friends each, that is about 34,000 ids, below the limit of 50,000. The engine removes user 5, their direct friends and duplicates, and counts how many friends each remaining person has in common with user 5.

The top 20 by common friends go back to the app. The whole query took one local read, one parallel round trip and 34,000 id reads, which is a few milliseconds, and it would take the same if the graph had ten times more users.

The user follows one of the suggestions. The write is recorded in the replicated log first, and a majority acknowledges it. Then both ends of the edge are written, even though they are on different shards.
The replicas apply the same log, so a failure of a shard loses nothing. Readers use a snapshot, so they see the new friendship on both ends or on neither.
